newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Thousands meet S.Africa's amnesty deadline.
newsitem.headline: Thousands meet S.Africa's amnesty deadline.

text.p: About 8,000 people, including Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, have met South Africa's deadline to seek amnesty for actions during three decades of apartheid race war, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission said on Sunday.
Commission spokeswoman Christelle Terreblanche told reporters that more than 2,000 applications had come in during the week leading up to the deadline at midnight on Saturday.
"We might just have hit a total of 8,000," she said, adding that among those applying last week were prison warders and members of African National Congress "self-defence units".
The units, composed of black township youths, were involved in political violence in the years ahead of South Africa's 1994 democratic elections.

An ANC spokesman said that Mbeki, Defence Minister Joe Modise, his deputy minister Ronnie Kasrils and Transport Minister Mac Maharaj were among applicants from the party. He said President Nelson Mandela was not on the list.
Few senior members of apartheid-era governments, with the exception of former police minister Adriaan Vlok, have applied.

The two surviving white presidents, P.W. Botha and F.W. de Klerk, have said they did nothing that could be construed as a crime or human rights violation. De Klerk said some individual security force officers appeared to have broken the law without authority.
Scores of former security branch policemen, including those responsible for the 1977 death of black activist Steve Biko, have asked for amnesty.

But only a handful of officers from the apartheid defence force have done so. Former defence minister Magnus Malan said that although he accepted moral responsibility he would not request legal absolution for fighting what he called Soviet expansionism.

No more than 100 members of Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi's Inkatha Freedom Party are reported to have applied. About 15,000 people were killed in a decade of feuding between Inkatha and the ANC which erupted in the mid-1980s and is still simmering.
The truth commission, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, has offered indemnity from criminal prosecution and from private litigation in a bid to lure perpetrators to reveal their secrets.
On Monday the ANC is to make the second part of a presentation to the commission on its actions and policy after it took up the armed struggle against white rule in 1960.

The commission is believed to have asked the party to clarify the execution of mutineers and suspected spies in camps in exile, to explain attacks on white civilians during the 1980s and to discuss its fight against Inkatha.
The ANC has repeatedly said it was conducting a just war which could not be compared morally with the actions of government security forces in enforcing apartheid.
The presentation on Monday follows one in August last year. The National Party of de Klerk and Botha will also make a follow-up presentation to the commission this week.
